utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the Prosecution would like to raise a preliminary matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honours. The Trial Chamber inquired at the end of the day yesterday whether the Prosecution accepted that there were quite a number of Serb victims in Sarajevo and then noted Ms. Edgerton's tacit assent. I hope it was clear that it was no way a ratification of the list or affirmation of the list presented by the witness. Instead as the Trial Chamber will recall, the Prosecution referred on several occasions when this general issue arose that we had been engaged in discussions with the Defence aimed at reaching agreement on a reliable minimum number of victims by ethnicity in Sarajevo in order to obviate the need for further court time regarding this issue. Those discussions have continued, and I believe have never been closer to resolution, but as the Defence and now the Trial Chamber are well aware, we do not accept the reliability of MFI 1216, D1216, and consider, instead, that reliable and accurate figures of Serb victims can emerge from the ongoing discussions with the Defence which have been long under way and hopefully are about to be resolved. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When the Chamber invited stipulation that at least larger numbers of Serb victims were -- fell victim in Sarajevo then in no way - and that was obvious from the cross-examination and that it was in no way understood as a stipulation that D1216 was an accurate and reliable document in this respect, and I think, Mr. Lukic, you would not have understood it in a different way, would you. MR. S. LUKIC: [Interpretation] The only thing that we think is that this list is correct and authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not my question, but at least you've now -- MR. S. LUKIC: [Interpretation] But in any case, I believe we should check all the data, all the information from that list, because it is not final as the witness himself has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether that needs to be done, I think I said yesterday something at the end of the -- at the session. The -- there was an admission of what has happened, although not reliable on the accuracy but that should be kept in mind also so that we don't start proving again which is not -- what is not in dispute. That is for the Defence, I think, as well. The parties are, under the Rules, under an obligation to seek to establish what is in dispute, and the Chamber tried to assist slightly in that respect yesterday. If the -- yes, the witness may be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tusevljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to remind you again that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. It was already a long time ago. Ms. Edgerton will now continue her cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tusevljak. Mr. Tusevljak, and Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We've actually brought a hard copy of D1216 for Mr. Tusevljak in his own language for him to leaf through as the cross-examination goes in an effort to speed things up, and I wonder if that might be shown to my friend, if he has no objection, and then be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you assist.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Great. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tusevljak, yesterday at transcript page 38492 to 38498, we looked at entries on page 3 of D1216 in the B/C/S versions, and, at the same time, we looked at entries at page 2 of a book by Dusan Zurovac, and that's 65 ter number 32976.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if we could just have those delayed again in B/C/S, we will then be able to display English language versions of the same pages we looked at yesterday, and Ms. Stewart has those pages in Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll wait for them to appear on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So for everyone and Mr. Tusevljak, these are the same documents we looked at at the beginning of your cross-examination yesterday, aren't they, and you agreed with me that the entries in D1216 at numbers 3, 4, 5, 6, and 9 were almost identical with the entries of the people, relating to the people by the same name in Mr. Zurovac's book; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could now move to these same pages in English, please. And those will also come up in Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it looks as if we have a technical issue, Your Honours, I would like to come back to this briefly, because I would like that ask to tender the pages of the Zurovac book. My friend, Mr. Registrar, he may be able to assist. So what we would be looking at, Mr. Registrar, is English page 3 of D1216, and ... Ms. Stewart advises me she might have it. Ah, wonderful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now we see in English on the screen on the left-hand side page 3 of D1216, and on the right-hand side, the English translation of B/C/S page 2, 65 ter number 32976, showing, in fact, what the witness has confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that being the case, Your Honour, I wonder if I might have this excerpt from 32976 admitted as a Prosecution Exhibit, please, with, of course, the cover page of the book so that we are able to see the author.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 32976 receives exhibit number -- MR. S. LUKIC: Sorry, I have an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We only have heard the number by now. Yes, what's the objection, Mr. Lukic. MR. S. LUKIC: [Interpretation] We don't know what is the probative value of the document being tendered because we don't see what they are trying to prove with this, because there has been no question asked in order to dispute or confirm the way in which the witness obtained this information, i.e., how his ministry obtained the information about what is included in the list of the missing and the people killed of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood the purpose of tendering this in evidence to be to demonstrate what was published in 2005 by one person is approximately the same language as what was later found in a list which was prepared by the government and not -- that that's the purpose of it. Have I understood the purpose well, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, not necessarily the intention of the ones who published the earlier list are decisive for the probative value. The objection is denied. The exhibit number, Madam Registrar, was.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number is P7525, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7525 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, Mr. Tusevljak, we also talked about a woman whose name appears at number, entry number 2597 on your list and her name is Jadranka Tenzera than name is English page 193 and B/C/S page 213 of D1216. Her father's name is listed in D1216 as Gradimir and her date of birth that appears in that document is listed as 1963. And we talked about her yesterday when I showed you a report in -- that was part of P867 which was the investigative file in relation to a shelling incident. Now, yesterday at transcript page 38519, I offered you a copy of her death certificate. The death certificate of the woman who died along with eight others in the shelling of Dobrinja on 4 February 1994 by the name of Jadranka Tenzera and I wanted to do that now. Could we please have 65 ter number 11229. So here in front of us is the English and the B/C/S copies of the death certificate for, as I said, the woman who was killed in the shelling of Dobrinja on 4 February 1994. Now you see in the top of the death certificate that her surname and first name are identical to the Jadranka Tenzera who appears at 2597 on your list. Her father's name is identical and she was born in 1963. Now, on this basis are you prepared to agree that this is the same person who appears on your list?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say anything about that because I don't have her case file and it's obvious that here in the explanation we've read yesterday was -- it was information from the centre from Belgrade. It's their information, and we indicated that clearly so without additional checks I cannot agree, because the reference there is to Vojnicko Polje and here it is to Dobrinja Jedan. The distance between the two is 3 or 4 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So what you're saying identical biographical data is not enough for you to confirm that this woman who appears at 2597 on your list is one and the same as the victim of the shelling of Dobrinja on 4 February 1994; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot confirm that for the reason I've explained. We've seen here that you have two completely different locations: Vojnicko Polje and Dobrinja 1. Two different places of death. It is reason enough to run additional checks. It's sufficient reason for more verification. We have only the -- that data and two different places of death, and that incident was not reported to the Ministry of Republika Srpska. We got this information from the centre for research into war crimes in Belgrade. We have two places of incident: Vojnicko Polje and Dobrinja 1. And it's enough for us to suspect that there may be additional checks needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one thing. You have several times referred to the information coming from the centre for the research into war crimes in Belgrade. Now, were you provided with just the outcome or do you also have the underlying documents on which they have based their reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we received documents on the basis of which they made their reports. We didn't receive original documents. We received copies of the documents underlying their reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would that mean that, for example, for this incident that you have an underlying report on Vojnicko Polje, what happened there on that same date with a person with the same name and the same year of birth? Would you be able to provide that underlying document which is, again, at the basis of the report from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That document was shown to me yesterday on the screen, a record of the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had it on the monitor yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean the document underlying the other place of the incident, and I think it was Belgrade that said that it happened at Vojnicko Polje. So would you have the underlying document from Belgrade which states that this lady died in Vojnicko Polje? Would be able to provide that document so as to verify what exactly was found and by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's truly impossible for me, with all these 3.300 names, to remember off the cuff today what is contained in each of the files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's not what I'm asking you. I'm asking you whether you would be able to provide the underlying documents - and I understood these were copies - the underlying documents which are at the basis of Belgrade's report that this lady died in Vojnicko Polje? Would you be able to provide that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We certainly have in her case file what we received from Belgrade, and we can provide that to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that would -- perhaps would be appreciated so that the verification which still may have to be done, to see whether it's identical purpose can be taken one step further. So if you would be so kind and perhaps you be given later a note with the details of the entry in your database and ... Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that this be tendered as a Prosecution Exhibit, Your Honour, and I'd just like to -- and, in fact, I must say, I'm advised by my colleague that this may be part of P867. Ms. Stewart is checking the translation. So if I could just reserve my request for the moment and -- with respect to this certificate, and I'll put it on the record as soon as I know, I can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, your request is put on hold and you may move on. And perhaps I immediately ask the witness now: Who's going to provide the exact name, date, et cetera, so that's able to -- would the Defence and the Prosecution perhaps do that together so just to provide the witness after ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please note down that what the Chamber would like to be provided with is the -- are the underlying documents -- yes. Madam Registrar will put it on a piece of paper - of number 2596 -- I beg your pardon -- 2597 of your list so as to be provided with the underlying documents supporting the Belgrade information which is contained in your list. Would you -- perhaps you make an arrangement with the Victims and Witness Section that you provide it to them so that it will finally land on our table, and the tables of the parties. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And this certificate is, I'm advised, part of P867, e-court English pages 63 and 64.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's hereby on the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tusevljak, after we discussed this woman and -- yesterday the case of Markale I where I pointed out to you at transcript pages 38520 to 38522 that your list included names of some victims of the February 1994 market-place shelling, you were asked whether you would agree that your list includes some Serb victims of shelling and sniping in Bosnian-held Sarajevo, and you said you could not. Now, that's at 38523, lines 21, to 38524, 16. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need a moment to find which number 3. You mean the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- cardinal numbers here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what Ms. Edgerton said. It has got nothing to do with the numbers on that list. The question, therefore, is whether you remember that you were asked whether you'd agreed that your list includes some Serb victims of shelling and sniping in Bosnian-held Sarajevo. Do you remember that you were asked about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember that, and I said that such persons should not be in this list. If somebody reported their victimisation, that reason was not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, based on your answer just now, can we understand that there was no intention to report Serb victims of shelling and sniping in Bosnian-held Sarajevo when you compiled this list? You excluded Serb victims of shelling and sniping in Sarajevo? Or you meant to exclude them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In Bosnian-held Sarajevo you were referring to, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. That was not our intention. We included in this list those persons that we realised had lost their lives. I have already mentioned our sources. Our intention was absolutely not to leave anybody out. List of Serb victims in Sarajevo, so it's only the information that we had available that was the criterion for us to put someone on the list, or not, and absolutely, the mode of death, et cetera, I have to tell you that many Serbs were killed at the actual front line because they were human shield there, they were digging trenches, they were work platoon members, et cetera, they were killed by Serb shells because they were intentionally exposed to that kind of fire and --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... now you keep going outside of the question that I ask. You just told us that you -- when you were asked yesterday whether you agreed your list included Serb victims of shelling and sniping in Bosnian-held Sarajevo, you just told us now that such persons should not be included in this list.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you totally misunderstood what I was saying. Our objective was as follows: On the basis of the information available at the moment we should compile a list of Serb casualties in Sarajevo and it was made exclusively on the basis of information, proof, evidence, that we had available because in every one of these explanations next to the name of each and every victim, we gave information as to roughly where we got this information, from the centre for war crimes in Belgrade or the centre for missing persons of Republika Srpska or some other archives or some witness states and so on and so forth. So it's on that basis that we actually -- we did not have any other objective.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's move on. Keeping in mind that you do not agree that your list includes Serb victims of shelling and sniping in Bosnian-held Sarajevo, I want to take you to some more examples on your list. Yesterday we talked about entry number 1316, a woman by the name - on your list on D1216 - a woman by the name of Vera Kovacevic and her name appears at entry 1316 on English and B/C/S page 109.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just try to fully understand. Ms. Edgerton, you referred to what the witness testified yesterday, that Serb victims from the Bosnian-held Sarajevo should not be on the list and today the witness said something different. And you now continue on the basis of what he said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we more or less, then, ignore what he said today which is contradicting what he said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, he indeed contradicted what he said yesterday and I'm trying through another example, Your Honour, to see if I can get to the bottom of the reasons for that contradiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But today I think the witnesses said: All victims are there. So if you want to establish that what he said yesterday is not correct, then he corrected himself today by saying, All Serb victims are to be on that list. So what you're now demonstrating is, on the basis of today's testimony, admitted by the witness, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What I noticed, Your Honour -- yes, Your Honour. So perhaps we'll just go back to this to try and have some more clarification. I'm very conscious of my time, Your Honour, and that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's why I tried to assist you, as a matter of fact. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Tusevljak, keeping in mind what is His Honour Judge Orie has said and the evidence that you've given, that this list was meant to include all victims, do you mean to say that this list does include victims of shelling, Serb victims of shelling and sniping, in Bosnian-held Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have told you - very clearly at that - that we made this list exclusively on the basis of the information we had available. So this list is not the only number of Serb victims in Sarajevo. There's a lot more. The reasons that you are referring to may be correct and may not be correct. Just as I said. Each and every name and surname that is placed here with the year of birth, it's a preliminary list. It hasn't been adopted anywhere because the commission that was supposed to work that was established for Sarajevo precisely because of this list never finished its job and they didn't want to deal with it in this way. They wanted to have proper files with proper evidence to show the suffering of all, not only Serbs in the territory of Sarajevo. So this commission no longer worked, and they never completed their mandate. Without any explanation. Although the High Representative in Bosnia-Herzegovina insisted several times that this should be completed. So that is the reason why this list was compiled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm stopping there because you're not answering the question. The simple question was whether that list was supposed to include or to exclude Serbs that fell victim in the Bosnian-held part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should include all victims, but this list is not final. That I said at the very outset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- this is a job that hasn't been completed, and it should include all victims. That is very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, it would not surprise you or us if Ms. Edgerton comes with names of persons - Serbs - who fell victim in Bosnian-held Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. There's a large number here of people who were killed in the territory of Sarajevo. However, the main thing is who the perpetrator is. And the Prosecutor keeps trying to impose who the perpetrator is. There is no doubt that these persons were victims, but the Prosecutor is trying to prove that it was Serb shells and Serb snipers that killed these people. That's where I degrees with the Prosecutor but she keeps insisting on that and that is her basic point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether that's her basic point or not is -- the Chamber will consider that. But I think the matter has been clarified, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, the examples that I've put to you so far from the 4th and 5th of February, 1994 relate to cases that have been tried and adjudicated by Chambers of this Tribunal. Do you disagree with me because you don't accept the findings of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, it's not that I can accept or not accept something that I'm not familiar with. First a person has to read something and then accept it or not accept it. That is a very basic thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go back to the woman I was speaking about initially and read something more. Vera Kovacevic, entry number 1316 in D1216 her name appears at English and B/C/S page 109. Father's name is Djordjo. Now your information relating to this woman, this victim, is that she's a teacher and that she was killed by an artillery shell in Sarajevo. Information from the centre for investigating crimes against the Serbian people, Belgrade. Now, having looked at this, I'd like us to go to 65 ter number 32993. This is an investigative file on the shelling that date in which not only Vera Kovacevic but three additional people were killed and nine wounded. And if we could please go over to -- if I can just have your indulgence for a moment. In B/C/S, the next page, this is the investigative official report on the shelling that day. And if you go down the list to page 2 in this report, both languages, you see that Vera Kovacevic, born in 1948, was one of the people in Sarajevo, Bosnian-held Sarajevo, who was killed by the shell that day. And she has the same date of birth as the woman listed at entry number 1316 on your list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We only see a year of birth.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Pardon me, again. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: She has the same year of birth as the woman who's identified on your list. Now, if we could go further to the very last page of the B/C/S version of this file. And, unfortunately, there's no English translation. And if we could just enlarge the entry on the bottom right-hand corner, this is the death notice for Vera Kovacevic, the woman who was killed in that shelling incident and her father's name appears in this entry, Djordje, which matches the biographical data of the woman who appears at entry number 1316 on your list. So the same person -- actually it's the second person with identical biographical data to an entry on your list is killed by a mortar shell in Bosnian-held Sarajevo and we have that information from contemporaneous documents. Are you prepared to concede on the basis of the identical biographical information and the information that she was killed in your list on the same day as this woman was killed by an artillery shell in Sarajevo, that's what your list says, are you prepared to concede that these two victims are one and the same.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is evident now. This is the first time I see this documentation, but also we didn't make any mistakes here. It says teacher, killed by a shell in Sarajevo, on 30th of August, 1993. You see here that it is the 30th of July, 1993 that there is this notice in the newspaper so there's one month difference and we also wrote that this is information for the centre for investigating crimes against the Serb people from Belgrade. Do you see somewhere that we wrote something different except for what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Witness, witness, you are defending yourself against what you assume to be allegations against you that you did something wrong. The simple question is whether you would agree that these are the same persons and you have answered the question by the first time part of it by saying that is clear to knee now, having looked at the material. That's an answer to the question. And carefully listen to the next question that Ms. Edgerton will put to you. And don't imagine all kind of allegations or accusations which are not, in any way, expressed by Ms. Edgerton. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, when we talked about Vera Kovacevic yesterday, you said at transcript page 38525 that when your information simply said "Sarajevo" as the place of the incident, you understood that that could refer to either Bosnian- or Bosnian Serb-held Sarajevo. Would you agree with me that we were only able to determine that this woman was killed by shelling in Bosnian-held Sarajevo as a result of additional investigation? The information on your list was deficient?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that we've seen all of this we can agree that she was killed by a shell and that's the only thing we can agree on. Whose shell? In which way? That I cannot see. This cannot be seen on the basis of all of this, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question was about the place in which this woman fell victim. My question is this: Can you agree that we're unable to determine, based on your information, where she fell victim without additional investigation; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I already said that this was preliminary and there have to be more investigations for this person. That is to say, all of these facts have to be looked at and then on the basis of that it should be established that --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you already answered the question. Thank you. I'd like to move on. I'd like to go to another case. And it's -- relates to entry number 1289 on your list. And the entry relates to a woman by the name of Vanda Mihajlo Knezevic and her name appears at English and B/C/S pages 107 of D1216.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if I could have this page of the investigative report, which is 65 ter number 32993, the last -- actually, what I'll do with -- in consultation with Ms. Stewart because I don't see a need to tender the whole file, is I'd ask for ... Your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We will create a 65 ter number for the excerpt of 32993, Your Honours. We'll create 32993a with the excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you tendered that. We'll wait until it's uploaded and then we'll decide on admission.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So we were talking about Vanda Knezevic, who is entry 1289 on your list and she appears at English and B/C/S page 107. Your information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. MR. S. LUKIC: It's not Vanda; it's Vera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let me see. Is the B/C/S -- let me just have a look. 2 --1289, even in the B/C/S version it seems to be Vanda, not Vera. We yesterday looked at another lady. MR. S. LUKIC: My mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now your information with respect to this individual is she was killed by an artillery shell on 12 April 1992 and the information comes from federal Oslobodjenje, and there's no more information as to the place of the incident. We have absolutely no idea where that took place based on the information you've got in your list; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So it could be anywhere. It could have been in Bosnian-held Sarajevo, could have been in Serb-held Sarajevo, it could have been anywhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we read this from Oslobodjenje, the newspaper clip --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... can we move the documents a bit to the left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we move it such that, in both languages, we can -- it's done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So my question is: Based on the information in your list, this could have taken place anywhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina; right.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because it's about Sarajevo. We also have other areas where there were Serb victims in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so there's no reason for us to repeat anything. There can be a technical error concerning persons who worked on the list but that should not be the case so this should just be persons who fell victim in Sarajevo. The only possibility is a technical error, but the percentage of the likelihood of that is negligible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question to you, sir is where do we see on this entry that had happened in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot see that either in this list, but I'm telling that you there is a file that accompanies each and every name. So we are talking about lists here that somebody made and we are not talking about files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you're not answering my question. You just told us that a few minutes ago about thousands of files you can't remember. You are telling us that this happened in Sarajevo and I'm asking you where on this document in this entry can we find that this incident happened in Sarajevo. So you're saying that you cannot find it there. Thank you so much. You've answered my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I cannot find it now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go to another entry -- actually, no, let's stay with this entry for a moment. Now you said that among the sources you consulted in carrying out your investigations, you would talk to family members who were searching for their nearest and dearest. Do you remember giving that evidence during your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In certain cases, people spoke to family members as well because there are reports to the commission for missing persons and we had that documentation available to, but it wasn't in each and every case, but in certain cases where we had the possibility to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's have a look at 65 ter number 32994, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is a report, an Official Note, on an interview with Mihajlo Knezevic and you'll recall that Mihajlo is listed at entry 1289 as being the father of Vanda Knezevic and in that interview, he makes clear that not only was his daughter killed by a shell in Sarajevo, in Bosnian-held Sarajevo, because that's where Mis Irbina Street is but her mother was killed at the same time. So -- and, by the way, not in April as your information indicates, but in July 1992. So even at the most basic level, there's no guarantee of the accuracy of the information in your list, is there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you cannot say that because you have -- have you been talking only about individual cases, and this list contains 3.300. You are talking out only a few. If we had more information or broader information, then we would have included this. This is data that we had at that time. Next to the name of this girl it says she was killed on the 12th of April and the information from the federal newspaper Oslobodjenje.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I see from Ms. Stewart that it's break time, Your Honour, and I would not want to go over that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you're still on track as far as time is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. Witness, you may follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Witness, I do understand that there has been contact with the VWS, and you'd very much like also to have the name and not only the number on your list, and I'll just find it for you. It was 2597.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. 2597. The name involved is Tenzera Jadranka, father's name Gradimir, born 1963. That's what we're talking about. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll receive any underlying documentation. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, you said a little while before we took our break that this commission for whom this list was prepared no longer works and that they never completed their mandate. So what I'd like to know from you is, then, can you tell us now who and how many people are actively engaged in working on the investigations relating to this list, if the commission doesn't operate any longer?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This work is now being done by the operative officers of the centre for public security of Sarajevo and there are six investigators. Not only these crimes but also war crimes, and these are auxiliary dossiers because their main purpose is to submit criminal complaints to the prosecutor's office of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's the work they are engaged in. And when they come across a new person or new evidence pertaining to these persons, this evidence is included in the relevant case file. They are not constantly engaged in this work, therefore, they only go back to it when they come across new evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So there's no active, focussed investigations going on related to anyone on this list. That's what you're telling us; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not the way it is. These are case files and all the persons on this list, because it's a huge number of people on the list, concerning these events, an official report was submitted to the prosecutor's office. The witness statements and the evidence that we have. And we have this official report submitted against the commander of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and against 280 other persons. Official reports were also submitted. These reports include information on the suffering of these persons. This work has not been completed --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and we have trials that are not completed yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I want to know what's going on now related to these people on this list. You keep talking about what has been completed and reports which have been submitted. What's going on now relating to Jadranka Tenzera, what's going on now relating to Vera Kovacevic, what's going on related to Vanda Knezevic, and everybody else on this list who you allege was victimised somewhere in Sarajevo. What's going on right now?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can begin with number 1 and then down the list and I can talk to you about each of the people. You have mentioned only four or five. I told you at the beginning, this is just an auxiliary resource in the work of the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska. We have case files for all the people killed. These case files are being supplemented every time when we come across new information and new evidence. The basic documentation concerning the suffering and the killings of these persons has been submitted either to the prosecutor's office of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the district prosecutors or the cantonal prosecutor. This is just an additional resource for the MUP. Our objective was not to create any kind of list. This list is just an aid in our work, just as have you your own lists and schedules. But we have criminal complaints and official reports submitted to the prosecutor. That is the basic criterion. The prosecutor's offices and the courts are there to continue working on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very frequently, we have orders from the prosecutors that concerns -- concerned these persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let's go back to the list to finish up because I want to finish up with this quite soon.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just before we do that, could I have 65 ter 32994 which we discussed before the break as a Prosecution Exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you not announcing that you upload an a version or is that a different one?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's a different one, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then 32994 receives what number, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P7527, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: My excuses. P7526.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7526 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's have a look at your list again and I want to look at the entry number 139 and it's on English and B/C/S page 14, related to Ratka Bilcar. We've been talking about shelling cases, and I want to have a look at a couple of more -- of different examples. You have a long description in your list relating to Ratka Bilcar, whose father's name is Borivoje, who was expelled from her apartment and taken to a detention facility in Sarajevo. And it's alleged in your list that she was killed at a check-point on the road to Dobrinja while attempting to leave Sarajevo. The probable motive was money. Now, I'd like us to have a look at 65 ter number 32942 in regard to this woman, Mrs. Bilcar. 32942 is a statement, an Official Note, on an interview with Dusan Bilcar who is the husband of Ratka Bilcar who was killed on 4 April 1993, according to him, by a sniper bullet fired from the direction of the positions of Serbian forces around Sarajevo. That she was -- and -- and Dusan Bilcar said that his wife was killed by a sniper shot to the head that day. So my question to you is this: You said in your testimony yesterday that you've never run away from corrections, and you have just told us that these files are being supplemented every time your investigators come across new information. So I want to know: Are you going to supplement the file on Mrs. Bilcar which says something completely different about her fate, which doesn't refer to a date of death with this new information.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But you know why? May I explain? Do you allow me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether Ms. Edgerton -- you said you would update it? If Ms. Edgerton is interested to know why would you do it although it may be obvious that new information should find its way in your list, but if she's interested, she will ask you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, if my friend sees a need, you can explain that to him in his redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to have this admitted as a Prosecution Exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 32942 receives exhibit number P7527, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. MR. S. LUKIC: [Interpretation] I apologise for reacting so late and objecting belatedly, but we do not see any references or information here to the effect that Mr. Bilcar signed this document confirming its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that. Is there a challenge to the authenticity; and, if so, on what basis? MR. S. LUKIC: Yes. [Interpretation] We cannot know whether he, indeed, gave this statement or not, when he was interviewed. We don't see his signature to confirm all of this. We only see the signature of the person who made this Official Note, but we don't even see the name of that person.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may respond, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And could you include in your response the source of where you obtained this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I corrected what I had initially said, explaining what 65 ter number 32942 is, by saying it was an Official Note on an interview with Dusan Bilcar. I made clear that it's not a statement. It's an Official Note on an interview with the man. I am simply and was simply offering that to Mr. Tusevljak as additional information relating to an incident for which the description is completely different to see if he was prepared to take this information on and update the file. It's not being tendered as a statement of Mr. Bilcar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, it's -- it's -- an exhibit is tendered and it's clear that it's an Official Note compiled by a person apparently of the Agency for Investigation documentation in Sarajevo. But my question was where did you get it from?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: OTP files received from the Agency for Research and Investigation in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, anything to add or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton, I see that this document is accompanied by two attachments. Are they also part of it? And can we perhaps have a look at them, if they are there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll speak with Ms. Stewart and I am sure that she'll get on to it in very short order, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps we wait to decide on admission until we have heard from you through Ms. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I want to move away a little bit from this topic and these individuals to go back to the list in a different way. Now, Mr. Tusevljak, when we spoke yesterday about soldiers on this list, you said -- and I asked you how many soldiers are on the list, you said: We did not make that kind of a distinction. But you said: It's very clear here it's always mentioned here if somebody is a soldier. But, in fact, Mr. Tusevljak, it's not always obvious in this list when somebody is a soldier and, in that regard, I want to direct you, first of all, to two names on your list who appear at English -- first at English and B/C/S page 15. The first one is number 150, and the person listed at that entry relates to -- is Radmila Bjelica who, it say was killed on 6 October 1993 at a place called Caklje on Mount Igman. And if we go over to the next page in B/C/S and have a look at entry number 157. At number 157 we see Tanja Bjelica, date of birth 1973 who was born in Trnovo, who was also killed on Igman. Now, having looked at those two entries, I'd like to us go over to 65 ter number 32950. So here what you see, Mr. Tusevljak, is a Sarajevo regular combat report to the Bosnian Serb army Main Staff dated 7 October 1994 reporting on the personal details of officers and soldiers killed in the attack. Now, if we could go over to the next page in this document in both languages, and we may be looking at page 3, please. And in B/C/S as well. Thank you very much. Now, if you go down on this list to number 15 and 16, we see that the two names we've just looked at on your list appear. The first one is Private Radmila Bjelica, daughter of Marinko, born 3 June 1974 in Trnovo. She's a signalswoman. The second one is the second name we just looked at, Tanja Bjelica, daughter of Slavko, born 1972 Sarajevo, also a signalswoman. And just to go down one further, number 17 on this list, Private Stojanka Golijanin is also appearing on your list, D1216 as entry number 611. They're all identified as signalswomen. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just note that number 16 on the previous list was born in 1973. Here they say 1972 is that just a typo or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't know where that typo might be, Your Honours, between Mr. Tusevljak's list and this SRK list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, of course, it would be fair to not suggest to the witness that these are identical persons. If there are differences there may well be, there may not be, but the witness who sees this for the first time might not notice that there are potentially differences and, therefore, I'd like to look at the entry for Golijanin to see whether that completely corresponds to what is found in this VRS report. And you said it was number --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 611, and it's in English and B/C/S page 53.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 53. One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's D1216.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Here, at least, the year of birth is corresponding.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: As is the father's name, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we have at least -- what we can see in the one document, and in the other there seems to be no ... no discrepancies.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And would Your Honours like to go back to pages 15 and 16 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The father's name is not identical. It says Petar and Petra.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would respectfully suggest that is likely a typo because Petra would be a woman's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But if you say it's identical, the father's name, you should refer to a possible typo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Tusevljak, here we've got a contemporaneous VRS document referring to three women by the same first name and surname as three identified in your list, killed in an attack on the same date as VRS soldiers. So, in fact, it's not always mentioned in the description of your list if somebody is a soldier, is it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I haven't made this list and all that you see here, all these soldiers were victims of a war crime. There was no combat operation then. It was a truce time at Caklje and the units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- were next to UNPROFOR units --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I didn't ask you about that. My colleague can raise that in his re-direct examination, if you want. My question to you was simple. It's not always mentioned in the description of your list whether somebody is a soldier, is it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You keep talking about my list, and I am talking about the list of the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska. I'm not the author of this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we are talking about your list, then it is the list that was brought by the Defence during your testimony and which you have worked on it one way or another, or at least that your department has worked on. That's what we call your list and that there's no one that suggests that you authored that list entirely. And then could we then go back to the question, because Ms. Edgerton asked you whether you would agree that it's not always clear from that list whether a victim was a soldier, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's evident that this fact is not always indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have this document as a Prosecution Exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 32950 receives exhibit number P7528, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7528 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, to go on to another area. When you talk about people who were victims, Serbs who were victims of war crimes vis-à-vis this list, did you include, did you intend to include people who fell victim to the actions of other Serbs? Just putting shelling and sniping completely aside for the moment.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In these lists, you will never see - or hardly ever - that it's mentioned who was responsible. I've already said that the list was made only on the basis of available documentation that is contained in files, and nothing else. There was no other motive. I really cannot understand this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let's see if we can get to -- if I can clarify this by going to another example. Now, let's go to 2783 on your list. That relates to an individual by the name of Novo Furtula and his name appears at English page 201 and B/C/S page 226. And maybe if we could -- if could you manage, if we could have both of them magnified a little bit. Now -- and if we could move everything a little bit over so that we see the descriptor on the right-hand side, please. It says that Novo Furtula born in Vlahovici was killed on 2.6.1992 in Dvorista. Now without anything further about this man's fate, we're unable to make a determination as to its relevance to any aspect of the case against General Mladic today, are we? We don't know how he was killed. We don't know who the perpetrators might have been. The information is deficient; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already told you, again, you are speaking about something that someone took out of a file, so whoever took this out of a file said born in Vlahovici, killed on the 2nd of June, et cetera. Killed how? Was it a sabotage group that killed that person? Whether it was something else, whether somebody planted a land-mine and whether he was killed by the enemy side, that is something that I cannot say. At this moment I cannot say this or that, but obviously this person is a victim --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- so here it says killed and somewhere else it says lost his life. So that's the only difference. People use the words they wanted: Killed in Hrasnica, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ... killed in Kazani so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you tell us where Dvorista is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dvorista is in the direction of Jahorina. It was under VRS control but a few times terrorist groups made incursions into that territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've just asked you where it was and you've told us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, in fact, Novo Furtula wasn't killed by a terrorist group who might have made an incursion. Could we have a look at D437, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And this document is a report on crimes for the months of August, September, October 1992 by the military prosecutor's office at the SRK ... for Han Pijesak. And if we could please go over to page 12 in both languages. The paragraph numbered 6 on this page indicates, Mr. Tusevljak, that Novo Furtula was one of three people who were killed in Pale municipality in the village of Dvorista by a man by the name of Vlatko Galinac who attached a bomb to the door of a weekend house. So here's, again, a contemporaneous document that shows the unreliability of the information in your list. This man, Novo Furtula, wasn't victimised by anyone who might have come from the enemy factions. The military prosecutor's office was dealing with him as a victim in a crime committed by a member of the VRS. That's what this document shows, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move onto another entry in your list, D1216, and it's going to be the last one dealing with this list. The entry is 1288, and it refers to Zelimir Knezevic and the entry appears at English and B/C/S page 107. Now, you see here that Zelimir Knezevic is simply listed as: Missing in Sarajevo. That's the extent of the information you have about him; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Information received from the office for missing persons. That's what it says afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right, let have a look with regard to this man, Zelimir Knezevic, at 65 ter number 32920. So here you've got a statement to the SDB to the MUP by a man named Muhamed Babic on 3 October 1992. Now if you could go over in both languages to page 2, please. In the penultimate paragraph in English and -- your indulgence for a moment. The final paragraph in B/C/S, you see how Mr. Babic describes what happened on 15 June 1992 in the morning when Veselin Vlahovic, known as Batko, and another man he didn't know came in a green Opel to their building and eventually saw Zeljko Knezevic and two other non-Serbs and took all three of them into the car. And if you go further down the paragraph, Muhamed Babic says: "After Dzonlic and the two other" -- pardon me. "After Knezevic and the two other non-Serbs were led away, we never saw them or heard anything of them again." Now, Mr. Tusevljak, you worked in criminal investigations since before the course of the war and you've worked in criminal investigations in Bosnian Serb-held territory from April 1992 throughout the war. You continued to work in criminal investigations. So you know who Batko was, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: He was a completely notorious man who was terrorising Grbavica in 1992, right, even the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know in the beginning of 1992, not throughout the year.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So Zelimir Knezevic who you say on your list was missing was taken away by Batko, according to this witness statement, and I'd like to show you -- I'd like to leave that statement for a moment and show you 65 ter number 32974.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, pardon me, I have the wrong number. Your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just your indulgence for a moment, Your Honours. Ms. Stewart is going to help me with the correct 65 ter number. Or P number perhaps. Could we have 65 ter number 12222, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this is the exhumations report for the year 2000 by Judge Ibrahim Hadzic and if we could go over to page 35 in English and page 44 in B/C/S, I'd appreciate that. So what you see here in front of you is that in September 1999 in Trebevic, if you go down to entry number 9 on this page, Zelimir Knezevic, the man who appeared at entry number 1288 on your list, was exhumed from a mass grave of 28 people. Trebevic -- pardon me. And now -- so, Mr. Tusevljak, here's a witness statement that's more contemporaneous than your list, and an exhumation report that's more contemporaneous than your list, that shows the man who you say went missing was taken by a notorious criminal operating in Bosnian Serb territory and his remains were recovered in what's now part of RS. So here's a couple of questions to you. You know, because you're a police officer involved in criminal investigations, that Batko was arrested a short time ago, tried and convicted in Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So while this related case with the same alleged perpetrator here was going on, you didn't do anything to update these files. Your team didn't do anything to update this file. SJB Sarajevo didn't do anything to update this file, did they? The file's not updated; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've already said, first of all, we put Zelimir Knezevic there on the basis of the information that we had. That is to say, the office of the missing persons. And that is stated clearly there. It's not that we were evading anything. We put on this list all the persons that we had aware of. What you're showing to me now is something that I see for the first time. It had been not made available to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. So you're not in any position to say whether or not there aren't other cases on your list where Serbs were victimised by Serb criminals, by VRS soldiers, by RS policemen. You're not in a position to confirm any of that, and this is just one example, isn't it? This is an example that shows that you can't confirm who the perpetrators might have been.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We do not refer to perpetrators anywhere, and I've already told you there are 3300 names, and we can go one by one and I can tell you whatever I know about each and every name. Now you're trying again to get me to answer questions on the basis of one name only.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So I want you to tell me what you, working in criminal investigations in 1992, did about Batko.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time -- or actually it was only at the end of 1992 that the crime prevention police started working. There weren't enough people there, there weren't enough operatives there. Our duty was only to deal with crimes that were not committed by members of the military, rather by civilians. Whenever we received information that any kind of crime had been committed, the on-site investigation team would go out on orders from the prosecutor or investigative judge and would carry out an on-site investigation and would provide information to the prosecutor's office in charge. As far as I know when the operation that was being -- was being prepared to arrest Vlahovic, this was seriously being prepared and he fled from Grbavica and from Republika Srpska and he was no longer accessible to us. We would have arrested him had we been in a position to do so. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That wasn't your priority at the time, was it? Your priority was investigating the theft of Golf cars from the Volkswagen factory in Vogosca; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right. We're talking about authority, powers. First of all, you are have to know what kind of powers we have and then can you say something. What the crime prevention police deals with and then what the national security department deals with, what the military security deals with, and so on and so forth. You know, we are talking about different powers in that period. So you cannot talk about priorities in the work of the crime prevention police, you can only talk about our powers at the time and also what the scope of our work was in 1992. It was not the investigation of such crimes. It was the national security department that was supposed to deal with that then. That's a completely different service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, you said you were on track as far as time is concerned, and I think had you one and a half hours for today.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could have probably five more minutes, Your Honour, I'll be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I'd -- I would have preferred if you would have asked it once you were running out of time rather than to wait until I respond. Five minutes is what you get.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, I just want to ask you one question, and it's -- but can you confirm to us that you know Dr. Svetlana Radovanovic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think I know her.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But in April 2009, you both took part in a conference in Moscow put on by the Russian Academy of Science?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you know her from that conference.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely cannot remember. There were over 100 people at that conference. Perhaps 150. I did meet some people, but to remember someone after having met that person just once, I mean, I meet people every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, that conference was about the ICTY, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that conference, I presented a paper, and it spoke about the NATO bombing of Republika Srpska. That was my topic --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I didn't ask you about that. The title of the conference was the Operation of the ICTY, its scope, results, and effectiveness; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. But you have my paper. I went there on account of that paper --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I was a presenter there and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Witness, Ms. Edgerton asked about the theme of the conference, not about what exactly your contribution was. She asked about the theme and, therefore, please try to focus your answers on what is asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have look at P7515, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what I'm going to show you, Mr. Tusevljak, is the conclusion to the collection of papers published that were presented at this conference. And if we could go over to English and B/C/S page 2, please. I think that's the wrong page in B/C/S, but I'll read the title because we ask to move on to the relevant paragraph. Thank you. What --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MR. S. LUKIC: I'm sorry that's not the B/C/S. It's the Russian language.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine. If we could, in Russian and in B/C/S the title of the next section that I'm going to direct you to says, "Conference participants have reached the following conclusions." Now if we go over to English page 3 and B/C/S page 7, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Russian page 7. My sincere apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, to show Russian to the witness only makes sense if he can read Russian. Are you able to read Russian? One second, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, very little. I did study Russian but that was a very long time ago. I cannot really use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then you'll receive it a translation of what Ms. Edgerton reads in the English language.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, now --

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Under this heading in the first paragraph it says: "Conference participants embraced the conclusion that the [sic] ICTY should be shut down immediately and that all its activity must be subjected to serious review. In addition to crude violations of international law and the [sic] ICTY's own rules of procedure, the principle of Rebus Sic Stantibus is in itself sufficient to effect the Tribunal's immediate abolition." Now, if we skip down, move down two paragraphs to the fourth paragraph on this page, it reads: "The responsibility of judges and other Tribunal personnel for violations of international law and of the Tribunal's own rules of procedure should be raised and actively pursued." Now, these are just two that I'm reading you of some of the core recommendations of the conference participants. These are your recommendations as well then, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that I was a participant here. I participated with my paper that had to do with the NATO bombing of Republika Srpska and the non-prosecution of that war crime. This is not the only gathering that I attended and that I participated in where the participants criticised the work of The Hague Tribunal. I do not see how somebody cannot be criticised or not criticised. I'm a policeman, a professional policeman. I just presented my paper, and there were many experts that attended here in international law, criminal law, Russian academicians, academicians from other countries. I was way down that chain. I already said yesterday that, as I did my work and my service, I studied the bombing and also the effect of depleted uranium on the citizens of Republika Srpska and Bosnia-Herzegovina and --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness you go far beyond the question but no foundation was laid yet. Did you at any point do you recognise that conversation, was -- were these conclusions put to the audience in your presence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see for the first time this paper --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you've answered my question. Did you ever vote in any way either in favour of or against these recommendations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't think I was even there when these conclusions were adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was read to you, do you share those recommendations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is only a part, one passage, I would need to read all. But if I can be honest, on many points regarding the Tribunal and their attitude to the cases where Serbs were the victims, that attitude was not adequate and it was deficient and we have the same situation today. I continue to fight in the prosecutor's office in Bosnia-Herzegovina and to date we have many crimes that have not been treated. There is not a single, final judgement in any of the major cases where the perpetrator was a Croat or a Bosniak. Very serious war crimes and I can tell you about all of these cases with many victims in Sarajevo, in Zenica, in Mostar, perpetrated by the 5th Corps, also cases in Srebrenica. With the MUP of Republika Srpska and the prosecutor's office we are working on bringing a new indictment against Naser Oric. There are many cases which were accessible to the OTP. That is my personal position. That's the way I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered my question. And I do understand that you added to what was not asked but that at least you have concerns about the way in which the crimes against Serbs were treated by Courts. Any further questions, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would like to come back to His Honour Judge Moloto related to Ratka Bilcar that he and Your Honours had a question about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the annexes to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Death certificate and a MRK, from what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, Your Honours. The complete -- we've located the complete Official Note and attachments and we uploaded into e-court the death certificate of Mrs. Bilcar as 65 ter number 32942 -- oh, the complete ERN. So for the Official Note and the death certificate attached it's 65 ter number 32942a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have it on our screen. I know what a death certificate is but what an MRK is -- I might the Chamber might want to have look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, there's no translation as yet for the death certificate yet, but we submitted it immediately a request for translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, oh, it was not MKR but MKU, and MKU is -- could we look at that attachment. Could we have a look at ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Ah, MKU could, I respectfully suggest, be the acronym for [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I now see that it's explained in the text. An excerpt from the MKU the register of death in her name and her death certificate. Yes, and these are the -- I take it that we'll MFI it awaiting it to be uploaded -- awaiting translation. Mr. Lukic. MR. S. LUKIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree. But I would also like to note that this document is connected not only to Ratka Bilcar but also the late daughter -- no, sorry. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and it also apparently at least, I see some description of apparently wounds having been found after a few years. I know more or less what vulnus trans-sclopetarium - that's Latin - refers to. We'll wait for a translation of the annexes. Madam Registrar, the number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter number 32920a receives MFI number P7529.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Give the 65 ter number again, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 32920a Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought it was 32942a.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There should be P7527 MFI.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, 27 is 32942 which was ... it is given 7527.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours if I could correct that, please. 65 ter number 32942a receives exhibit number P7527, Your Honours. And the exhibit number P7529 will be vacated again. My excuses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's hereby on the record --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, just two more exhibit-related housekeeping matters that I haven't tendered yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I first wanted to MFI this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I wanted to ask Mr. Lukic, since the annexes seems to be full of stamps and signatures, et cetera, does the objection to the authenticity of the Official Note itself stand? MR. S. LUKIC: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly because the accompanying documentation relates to the excerpt from the register of death and has nothing to do with what Mr. Dusan Bilcar provided as information contained in the Official Note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you don't see any link between what he describes as the cause of death and what most likely in your language is explained in the annex? I mean, I read only the bullet wound. I did not read the word "capitis," which if my Latin is still okay stands for at the head. But if you say it stands, then we'll decide on it. If you want to add anything to it, then you have an opportunity to do so. Otherwise we'll proceed. MR. S. LUKIC: [Interpretation] Right. But from the Official Note, we do not see who compiled the Official Note or whether it was made based on what Mr. Dusan Bilcar said.
